⟦p:jude_1756|Jude⟧ is the last of the short general letters before Revelation, and it comes from another member of ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' own family. The writer calls himself Jude, a servant of ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus Christ⟧ and a brother of ⟦p:james_719|James⟧. His name is Judas, the Greek form of Judah and a common Jewish name, and English translations usually call him Jude to distinguish him from ⟦p:judas_1760|Judas Iscariot⟧.

The ⟦p:james_719|James⟧ he mentions is James the brother of the Lord, the leader of the church in ⟦l:jerusalem_636|Jerusalem⟧ and the writer of the letter of James. So ⟦p:jude_1756|Jude⟧ too was one of ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧' brothers. The Gospels name four of them, James, ⟦p:joseph_1710|Joseph⟧, ⟦p:peter_2745|Simon⟧ and Judas, and record that during Jesus' ministry they did not believe in him. After the resurrection his brothers appear among the believers in Jerusalem, and ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ mentions the Lord's brothers travelling in the work of the gospel. Jude does not call himself the brother of Jesus. He describes himself instead as his servant, and identifies himself through James, the better known of the two. A story from the second century tells of Jude's grandsons, farmers with hands hardened by work, brought before the emperor Domitian and questioned about Christ's kingdom.

His readers knew the Scriptures and traditions of Israel well. The letter belongs to the second half of the first century, and it is closely related to Second ⟦p:peter_2745|Peter⟧, since a long passage appears in both in similar form.

The occasion is urgent. ⟦p:jude_1756|Jude⟧ explains that he had meant to write a letter about the salvation he and his readers share, but news has forced him to change course. Certain men have slipped into the community unnoticed. They turn the grace of God into an excuse for immorality, reject authority, and deny ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus Christ⟧ as Master and Lord. They take part in the church's love feasts, the shared meals at which believers gathered, and use them for their own ends.

⟦p:jude_1756|Jude⟧ is a vivid writer who likes to group things in threes. He recalls three examples of judgment from Israel's history, and three figures from the Old Testament who went the wrong way: ⟦p:cain_533|Cain⟧, ⟦p:balaam_593|Balaam⟧ and ⟦p:korah_1795|Korah⟧. He piles up pictures from the natural world to describe the intruders: hidden reefs, clouds without water, fruitless trees, wild waves, wandering stars. He tells of the archangel ⟦p:michael_2068|Michael⟧ disputing with ⟦p:satan_2476|the devil⟧ over the body of ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, and he quotes the prophecy of ⟦p:enoch_1192|Enoch⟧, the seventh from ⟦p:adam_78|Adam⟧, about the Lord coming with myriads of his holy ones.

Yet the letter does not end in denunciation. It turns to the readers themselves, calls them to build one another up and to show mercy to those who doubt, and closes with one of the most beautiful words of praise in the New Testament.

After a brief greeting to those called and kept by God, the letter turns at once to its reason for being. ⟦p:jude_1756|Jude⟧ had intended to write about the salvation he and his readers share, but he has heard that intruders have crept in among them, and he must urge them instead to contend for the faith.

He reminds them of what they already know: the generation that came out of ⟦l:egypt_362|Egypt⟧ and perished in the wilderness, angels who abandoned their place, ⟦l:sodom_1107|Sodom⟧ and ⟦l:gomorrah_489|Gomorrah⟧. Then he describes the intruders in a rapid stream of images, setting them in the line of ⟦p:cain_533|Cain⟧, ⟦p:balaam_593|Balaam⟧ and ⟦p:korah_1795|Korah⟧, and quoting ⟦p:enoch_1192|Enoch⟧'s prophecy of the Lord coming in judgment.

In the final verses ⟦p:jude_1756|Jude⟧ speaks directly and tenderly to his beloved readers, and the letter ends with a soaring word of praise to the God who is able to keep them from stumbling.
